query: For initially solid FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles exposed to the premelting and melting regime, the limited understanding of their thermal response prevents clear definition of their usable temperature range and behavior during high-temperature synthesis. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs the onset and progression of their phase transition and why? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, relevant boundary conditions, supporting evidence from prior nanoparticle studies, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In FeNiCrCoCu high‐entropy alloy nanoparticles, the onset and progression of the phase transition in the premelting/melting regime is primarily governed by thermally activated surface and grain‐boundary diffusion that promotes elemental segregation—especially of the low‐melting-point component (Cu) and residual impurities—to form a thin liquid layer. This locally reduced melting point then propagates into complete melting.
generation.material_initial_state: Solid, homogeneous FeNiCrCoCu high‐entropy alloy nanoparticles with minimal pre‐existing phase separation.
generation.intervention: Heating the nanoparticles under controlled inert atmosphere conditions with a fixed and reproducible heating rate, while comparing two sets prepared with different impurity levels (e.g., high purity vs. trace impurity added).
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted in an inert gas (e.g., argon) atmosphere; heating rates maintained constant; identical nanoparticle size distributions; temperature range spanning the premelting up to full melting regime.
generation.structural_mediator: The nanoparticle surfaces and grain boundaries, where enhanced atomic mobility allows for the segregation and enrichment of Cu and impurities.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures approaching the melting regime, thermally activated atomic diffusion leads to the preferential migration of Cu and impurity atoms to the surfaces and grain boundaries. This segregation lowers the local melting point (premelting) at these regions, initiating the formation of a liquid-like interfacial layer that serves as a pathway for the progression into bulk melting.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles with higher impurity concentrations or enhanced surface segregation will exhibit a lower onset temperature for liquid layer formation, observable as early premelting features (e.g., via DSC endotherms and TEM imaging of liquid-like surfaces) compared to purer samples, with the progression toward complete melting occurring through the growth and coalescence of these liquid regions.
generation.baseline: Behavior of pristine, compositionally homogeneous, as-synthesized FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles under identical thermal treatment.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable under controlled inert atmospheres and when nanoparticle size, heating rate, and composition (aside from deliberate impurity variation) are kept constant; deviations in these factors may introduce additional complexities.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative impact of impurity concentration and the degree of Cu segregation on the local melting temperature remains to be determined. Microstructural inhomogeneities in nanoparticles might also affect the onset kinetics, implying that the size, shape, and defect distribution could modulate the observed effects.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform in situ high-resolution TEM experiments coupled with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) mapping on heated FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles. Two sets of samples (one with deliberately introduced trace impurities and one high-purity control) would be heated at an identical rate in a controlled inert atmosphere. Real-time imaging and compositional mapping would track the formation of any liquid-like layers at the surfaces and along grain boundaries.
measurements: Onset temperature of detectable liquid layer formation via TEM imaging.
Local compositional profiles (especially for Cu and impurities) at the nanoparticle surfaces and interfaces using EDS.
Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) data to correlate thermal events with structural changes.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experiments show that no preferential surface or grain-boundary segregation of Cu/impurities occurs before the melting transition, or if similar melting-onset temperatures and morphologies are observed in both high-purity and impurity-introduced samples without evidence for a pre-melting liquid layer, then the hypothesized mechanism would be falsified.

Abstract: AbstractInvestigation into non-equiatomic high-entropy alloys has grown in recent years due to questions about the role of entropy stabilization in forming single-phase solid solutions. Non-equiatomic alloys have been shown to retain the outstanding mechanical properties exhibited by their equiatomic counterparts and even improve electrical, thermal, and magnetic properties, albeit with relaxed composition bounds. However, much remains to understand the processing–structure–property relationships in all classes of so-called high-entropy alloys (HEAs). This is demonstrated by cooling an equiatomic CrMnFeCoNiCu alloy from the melt steadily over 3 days (cooling rate ~4 °C/h). The more the better: on the formation of single-phase high entropy alloy nanoparticles as catalysts for the oxygen reduction reaction†

Abstract: AbstractHigh entropy alloys (HEAs) are an important new material class with significant application potential in catalysis and electrocatalysis. The entropy-driven formation of HEA materials requires high temperatures and controlled cooling rates. However, catalysts in general also require highly dispersed materials, i.e., nanoparticles. Only then a favorable utilization of the expensive raw materials can be achieved. Several recently reported HEA nanoparticle synthesis strategies, therefore, avoid the high-temperature regime to prevent particle growth. In our work, we investigate a system of five noble metal single-source precursors with superior catalytic activity for the oxygen reduction reaction. Combining in situ X-ray powder diffraction with multi-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy, we address the fundamental question of how single-phase HEA nanoparticles can form at low temperatures. Origin of age softening in the refractory high-entropy alloys

Abstract: AbstractRefractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are emerging materials with potential for use under extreme conditions. As a newly developed material system, a comprehensive understanding of their long-term stability under potential service temperatures remains to be established. This study examined a titanium-vanadium-niobium-tantalum alloy, a promising RHEA known for its superior high-temperature strength and room-temperature ductility. Using a combination of advanced analytical microscopies, Calculation of Phase Diagrams (CALPHAD) software, and nanoindentation, we investigated the evolution of its microstructure and mechanical properties upon aging at 700°C. Trace interstitials such as oxygen and nitrogen, initially contributing to solid solution strengthening, promote phase segregation during thermal aging. As a result of the depletion of solute interstitials within the metal matrix, a progressive softening is observed in the alloy as a function of aging time.
